title: How James Talarico Won
author: Youth Outsider Editorial Team
dek: Texas had not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. On Tuesday, a 37-year-old former middle school teacher beat Ken Paxton by 12 points. Here is how he did it.

body:
Donald Trump carried Texas by 14 points in 2024. Two years later, the state elected James Talarico to the U.S. Senate, 55% to 43%, [according to county returns compiled by Newsweek](https://www.newsweek.com/ken-paxton-james-talarico-texas-senate-election-results-12667994). The Associated Press called the race shortly after 10 p.m. It was the first Democratic Senate win in Texas since 1988, and the first time Democrats had won any statewide race there since 1994, [The Texas Tribune reported](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/11/03/texas-ken-paxton-james-talarico-us-senate-elections-2026/).

Talarico is a four-term state representative from the Austin area and a Presbyterian seminarian with no federal experience. He won by a wider margin than any public poll had predicted. Part of that was the year, which was a bad one for Republicans everywhere. Most of it came from the choices on each side.

## He got the opponent Democrats wanted

Ken Paxton, Texas's attorney general, entered the race carrying more baggage than almost any Senate candidate in the country. He had been indicted on felony securities fraud charges, which were later dropped under a pretrial diversion deal. He had been the subject of a federal investigation. He had been impeached by the Texas House and acquitted by the state Senate. And his wife, state Sen. Angela Paxton, had filed for divorce, accusing him of adultery.

Republican leaders warned that Paxton could lose the seat. Sen. John Cornyn, the incumbent he was challenging, said in August that Paxton was *"lazy and doesn't raise money."* But Trump endorsed Paxton a week before the May runoff, and Paxton beat Cornyn by 28 points.

By the fall, Paxton's ratings were worse than Trump's and worse than those of other statewide Republicans, according to the Tribune. Many of his own supporters said they were voting against Talarico more than for him.

## He survived a hard primary first

Talarico's own nomination was not guaranteed. U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, a nationally known progressive from Dallas, entered the race on the last day of filing in December, and former Rep. Colin Allred dropped out. Talarico beat Crockett by six points in March.

The primary left wounds. Some Black voters who had backed Crockett said Talarico had not yet earned their support. In September, he pledged $25 million toward Black voter turnout, and on election night, returns from majority-Black areas showed no sign of a drop-off.

## He talked about faith, and meant it

Most Democrats avoid talking about religion. Talarico built his career on it. He first went viral for clips of himself quoting scripture in the Texas House, including in a debate over a bill requiring the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms, which he called un-Christian. He launched his Senate campaign in September 2025 with a video about loving God and neighbor and said it was *"time to start flipping tables,"* a reference to Jesus driving the money changers out of the temple.

The message reached people who don't usually listen to Democrats. In July 2025, Talarico spent three hours on Joe Rogan's podcast. Rogan, who backed Trump in 2024, ended by telling him, [*"James Talarico, you need to run for President. We need someone who is actually a good person."*](https://time.com/7304119/joe-rogan-james-talarico/)

Republicans attacked him on the same ground. Trump went after a 2021 podcast in which Talarico called himself a "Christian who hates Christianity," [according to The Christian Post](https://www.christianpost.com/news/10-christian-democrats-seeking-election-on-nov-3.html). It did not stick. Talarico's argument, that his faith asked him to care about the poor and the sick, gave him a way to talk about policy without sounding like a national Democrat.

## He reached across, and talked about costs

Voters ranked the economy and the cost of living as their top issue, with gas and grocery prices high across the state. Talarico ran on both, and on corruption, a word that did a lot of work against Paxton.

He also went after Republicans directly. He courted Cornyn voters and moderate Republicans, won endorsements from some of them, and distanced himself from some of his past comments. Heading into September, he led independents by more than 20 points, according to the Tribune.

## He raised more and spent smarter

The race was the most expensive nonpresidential contest on record, with nearly [$590 million](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/11/03/texas-ken-paxton-james-talarico-us-senate-elections-2026/) in ad spending across the primaries and general election, according to AdImpact. Republicans spent more than $280 million on ads, and Elon Musk alone put more than $200 million into the effort to elect Paxton.

Talarico was outspent nearly two to one in the general election, but he had more money of his own. He raised $27 million in the first three months of the year, a first-quarter record for a Senate candidate in an election year. Because candidates pay lower rates for TV ads than outside groups do, his money bought more airtime. He went on the air early and stayed there.

## Latino voters came back

The biggest shift came along the border. In 2024, Latino voters in South Texas moved sharply toward Trump. This year, they moved back. In Webb County, home to Laredo, Trump won 51% in 2024. Paxton won 25%, [Fox 26 Houston reported](https://www.fox26houston.com/news/2026-election-massive-latino-turnout-border-county-reversal-fuel-democratic-wins). In Maverick County, which Trump won with 59%, Paxton got 28%. In Starr County, which is 97% Latino, the margin swung more than 70 points toward Talarico, [according to The Bulwark](https://www.thebulwark.com/p/latino-fury-how-anti-ice-fervor-helped-democrats-midterms-blue-wave-immigration-economy). NBC's exit poll found that [61% of Latino men](https://www.newstribune.com/news/2026/nov/06/how-latino-voters-helped-secure-blue-victories/) in Texas voted for him.

Many Latino voters and leaders pointed to immigration enforcement. Trump's deportation drive brought masked agents and raids into Latino communities, and in 2025 the Supreme Court lifted a lower-court ban on agents considering "apparent race or ethnicity" during patrols, a ruling rights groups said [effectively allowed racial profiling](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/30/on-the-us-border-in-texas-trump-deportation-drive-galvanises-midterm-vote). In an ACLU of Texas poll, 64% of respondents said ICE's tactics had gone too far. *"The difference is ICE and the mass deportation campaign,"* said Rep. Joaquin Castro of San Antonio. Even some Republicans blamed their party's messaging: GOP strategist Giancarlo Sopo argued that lumping "criminal illegals" together with immigrants working through the legal system was turning Hispanic voters away. Talarico leaned in, calling ICE a *"secret police force"* with *"zero accountability."*

Prices mattered too. Cost of living remained Latino voters' top concern, and many said they were struggling to pay their bills.

Turnout helped. About 1.6 million Latinos voted in Texas, according to the civil rights group LULAC, nearly double the number in the last midterm. Talarico also outspent Paxton and his allies on Spanish-language ads, about $2.6 million to $1.4 million.

The suburbs went his way too. Talarico won Collin County, north of Dallas and home to more than a million people, by 12 points, and flipped Kaufman County, which Trump had carried.

## What comes next

*"We were the underdogs in this race,"* Talarico told supporters in Austin on Tuesday night. He called for [*"a politics of love,"*](https://www.ksat.com/news/local/2026/11/04/full-speech-talarico-vows-a-politics-of-love-in-speech-after-historic-senate-win/) said the win was *"not about the Democratic Party or the Republican Party,"* and ended where his campaign began: *"Texas, it's time to start flipping tables."*

Paxton conceded the same night. *"Let me start off by congratulating James Talarico,"* he said, adding that he would be praying for him.

Talarico takes office in January as one of the youngest members of the Senate, from a state Democrats have spent three decades trying to win. Rogan already told him to run for president. After Tuesday, he won't be the last.
